title: Next.js App Router architecture
description: Explore how the Next.js App Router organizes your application using folders, layouts, and server-first rendering.

data.text: The **App Router** is Next.js's modern way to build applications. Instead of one big file for each page, you organize your app inside folders where each folder represents a route. The `app` directory contains **layouts**, **pages**, and **templates** that wrap your content and share UI across routes.

Think of it like a set of nested boxes. The outer box is the root layout. Inside it, each folder adds another layer. Files named `page.tsx` define what users see at that URL. Files named `layout.tsx` define the shared chrome around it — navigation, sidebars, or footers. Files named `loading.tsx` show a fallback while content loads.

items: `app/layout.tsx` wraps every page in the same folder
`app/loading.tsx` shows a fallback while a page or nested layout loads

data.title: Mental model
data.text: The closest match is a file-system router. The key difference is that the App Router treats every route as a **Server Component** by default. That means the initial HTML is rendered on the server, which keeps the client bundle small.

terms.definition: A UI shell that wraps one or more pages and preserves state during navigation.
The unique UI for a route. Only one active page renders at a time per route segment.
Like a layout, but it re-mounts on every navigation instead of preserving state.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: The App Router is folder-based, not file-based like the Pages Router.
Layouts share UI across routes without repeating markup.
Every page is a Server Component by default.
data.takeaway: Mastering the App Router means understanding how folders, layouts, and server-first rendering work together.
